notes: Appendix A of RFC 6902 is the specification's own worked example set, A.1 through A.16, and is transcribed here verbatim. The cases after it are drawn from the normative text of sections 4 and 5: they are the rules an implementation can pass all of appendix A while still getting wrong, because appendix A never exercises them.

field_guide.document: The target document the patch is applied to.
field_guide.patch: The patch document, as parsed JSON.
field_guide.patch_text: Present instead of patch when the patch cannot be represented as parsed JSON, for instance because it has a duplicate member name. The runner parses this string.
field_guide.expect: apply when the patch must succeed, error when a conforming implementation must report an error and leave the target document alone.
field_guide.result: Present only when expect is apply: the document the patch must produce. Compared member-order-insensitively, since RFC 8259 gives object members no order.
field_guide.check_unchanged: Present only on error cases that specifically test atomicity: the target document is re-read after the failure and must still equal its original value.

cases.title: A.2 Adding an array element
cases.notes: add at an existing array index inserts before that element, it does not replace it.

cases.title: A.7 Moving an array element
cases.notes: The destination index is interpreted against the array after the removal, which is why the result is not ["all", "cows", "grass", "eat"].

cases.title: A.10 Adding a nested member object
A.11 Ignoring unrecognized elements
cases.notes: A member the specification does not define is ignored rather than rejected, which keeps the format extensible.

cases.title: A.12 Adding to a nonexistent target
cases.notes: add creates the last path segment only. The parent /baz does not exist, and add must not conjure it.

cases.title: A.13 Invalid JSON Patch document
cases.notes: The operation object names op twice. Stored as text because a corpus that stored it as parsed JSON would have had to pick one of the two.

cases.title: A.14 Escape ordering
cases.notes: ~0 is expanded before ~1, so /~01 names the member ~1 and not the member /.

cases.title: A.15 Comparing strings and numbers
cases.notes: test compares JSON values, so the string "10" is not equal to the number 10.

cases.title: A.16 Adding an array value
cases.notes: The - token appends, and an array value is appended as one element rather than spliced in.

cases.title: A patch whose second operation fails leaves the document alone
cases.paragraph: If a normative requirement is violated by a JSON Patch document, or if an operation is not successful, evaluation of the JSON Patch document SHOULD terminate and application of the entire patch document SHALL NOT be deemed successful.
cases.notes: The first operation succeeds in isolation. An implementation that mutates the caller's document in place as it goes will leave /b behind after the failure.

cases.title: move must reject a destination inside its own source
cases.paragraph: The from location MUST NOT be a proper prefix of the path location; i.e., a location cannot be moved into one of its children.
cases.notes: An implementation built as remove-then-add loses the destination's parent when the source is removed, and typically reports a confusing secondary error or silently produces nonsense.

cases.title: test treats 1 and 1.0 as the same number
cases.paragraph: numbers are considered equal if their values are numerically equal.
cases.notes: Numeric equality is by value, not by lexical form and not by storage type.

cases.title: test treats objects with reordered members as equal
cases.paragraph: objects: are considered equal if they contain the same number of members, and if each member can be considered equal to a member in the other object, by comparing their keys (as strings) and their values (using this list of type-specific rules).
cases.notes: An implementation that compares two objects by serializing both and comparing the text fails this, because serialization preserves member order.

cases.title: add at an index equal to the array length appends
cases.paragraph: An element to add to an existing array - whereupon it is added at the index... The specified index MUST NOT be greater than the number of elements in the array.
cases.notes: Index 1 in a one-element array is the one-past-the-end position, which is legal and equivalent to -.

cases.title: add beyond one past the end of the array is an error
cases.paragraph: The specified index MUST NOT be greater than the number of elements in the array.
cases.notes: Index 2 in a one-element array would leave a hole, which JSON arrays cannot represent.

cases.title: remove of a member that is not there is an error
cases.paragraph: The target location MUST exist for the operation to be successful.
cases.notes: remove is not idempotent in JSON Patch. An implementation that rebuilds the object while skipping the named key cannot tell a removal from a no-op.

cases.title: path must be a string
cases.paragraph: Additionally, operation objects MUST have exactly one 'path' member. That member's value is a string containing a JSON-Pointer value.
cases.notes: An accessor that coerces rather than type-checks turns the number 1 into the pointer "1", which is then not even a well-formed pointer.

cases.title: remove of a member name that needs JSON string escaping
cases.paragraph: The remove operation removes the value at the target location.
cases.notes: An implementation that rebuilds an object by concatenating '"' + key + '":' emits invalid JSON for this member name and then fails to re-parse its own output.

cases.title: add without a value member is an error
cases.paragraph: The operation object MUST contain a 'value' member whose content specifies the value to be added.
cases.notes: A missing member must be an error rather than a silently substituted null.
